blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A competing event is an event whose occurrence prevents the event of interest from happening. The cumulative incidence function (CIF), F_k(t), is the probability of having event type k by time t before any competing event. It is estimated by the Aalen–Johansen estimator. Two regression approaches exist: the cause-specific hazard model (a Cox model for the event of interest, with competing events censored) and the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard model (which models the CIF directly).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Suppose the event of interest is sputum culture conversion among patients on treatment for drug-resistant TB, and some patients die first. A dead patient cannot convert. If you censor deaths and compute 1 − Kaplan–Meier for conversion, the method assumes the dead patients would have gone on to convert at the same rate as the survivors. That describes an imaginary world without death. In the real cohort, 1 − KM overstates the proportion who convert. Using the Kaplan–Meier function “results in estimates of incidence that are biased upward, regardless of whether the competing events are independent of one another” (Austin et al., 2016).

The CIF fixes this. At each conversion time, the probability of converting now is the probability of still being event-free of both kinds just before, times the fraction of the at-risk set converting now.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Let S(t) be the Kaplan–Meier estimate treating any event (conversion or death) as the event: the probability of being free of both. At a conversion time tⱼ, with nⱼ at risk and d₁ⱼ conversions,

P(convert at tⱼ) = S(tⱼ₋) × d₁ⱼ/nⱼ, where S(tⱼ₋) is S just before tⱼ.

Summing: F₁(t) = Σ over tⱼ ≤ t of S(tⱼ₋) × d₁ⱼ/nⱼ. By construction, F₁(t) + F₂(t) + S(t) = 1: everyone has converted, died first, or neither. 1 − KM for conversion instead multiplies (1 − d₁ⱼ/nⱼ) factors with deaths censored, so each dead patient’s share is carried forward as if they could still convert. Its value therefore exceeds F₁(t) once a death has occurred, and 1 − KM for conversion plus 1 − KM for death can add to more than 1.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Ten patients, weeks on treatment (C = converted, D = died before conversion, + = censored alive and unconverted): 2C, 3D, 4C, 5D, 6C, 7+, 8C, 9D, 10C, 12+.

3 D 9 0.900 — 0.100 0.100
4 C 8 0.800 0.100 0.200 0.213
5 D 7 0.700 — 0.200 0.213
6 C 6 0.600 0.100 0.300 0.344
7 + 5 0.500 — 0.300 0.344
8 C 4 0.500 0.125 0.425 0.508
9 D 3 0.375 — 0.425 0.508
10 C 2 0.250 0.125 0.550 0.754
  1. S(t) for “free of both” steps down at every C and D: 1 × 9/10 = 0.900; × 8/9 = 0.800; × 7/8 = 0.700; × 6/7 = 0.600; × 5/6 = 0.500; (censoring at 7: no step); × 3/4 = 0.375; × 2/3 = 0.250; × 1/2 = 0.125.
  2. CIF of conversion at 12 weeks = 0.100 + 0.100 + 0.100 + 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.550.
  3. CIF of death before conversion, by the same rule at weeks 3, 5 and 9: 0.900/9 + 0.700/7 + 0.375/3 = 0.100 + 0.100 + 0.125 = 0.325.
  4. Check: 0.550 + 0.325 + 0.125 (neither yet) = 1.000.
  5. 1 − KM with deaths censored: 1 − (9/10 × 7/8 × 5/6 × 3/4 × 1/2) = 1 − 0.246 = 0.754. It overstates conversion by 0.754 − 0.550 = 0.20, because it treats the three dead patients as if they could still convert.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Which regression model? The cause-specific hazard model is an ordinary Cox model for conversion with deaths censored. It estimates the effect of a covariate on the conversion rate among patients still alive and unconverted: an aetiological question. The Fine–Gray model estimates the effect of a covariate on the cumulative incidence of conversion, that is, on the actual proportion who convert in a population where people also die. Its HR (the subdistribution HR) is harder to read as a rate, because people who have already died stay in its risk set. Austin et al. (2016) summarise: the cause-specific model “may be better suited for addressing etiologic questions”, the CIF model “for estimating a patient’s clinical prognosis”. Lau et al. (2009) add that the choice should be “guided by the scientific question”. The two HRs can differ: a treatment that lowers only the death hazard leaves the cause-specific HR for conversion at 1, yet raises the cumulative incidence of conversion, because it keeps more patients alive to convert.

The CBHI cohort as a sensitivity analysis. Suppose moving out of the district ends CBHI membership by a route the scheme does not count as dropout. Moving is then a competing event, not censoring. The §14.7 Cox model already treats movers as censored, so its HR of 0.58 is the cause-specific HR, and it stands for the aetiological question. What changes is the proportion who drop out: 1 − KM gives 0.42 by 24 months (1 − 0.58), the CIF gives 0.40. With only 18 movers the difference is small; when competing events are common (deaths in an elderly cohort), it is large.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(cmprsk)
# status: 1 converted, 2 died, 0 censored
tb <- data.frame(week   = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12),
                 status = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0))
timepoints(cuminc(tb$week, tb$status, cencode = 0), c(4, 8, 12))$est
co <- read.csv("data/cohort_dropout.csv")
co$status3 <- ifelse(co$dropout == 1, 1,
                     ifelse(co$censor_reason == "moved away", 2, 0))
ci <- cuminc(co$time_months, co$status3, group = co$intervention,
             cencode = 0)
round(timepoints(ci, 24)$est, 3)
ci$Tests
fg <- crr(co$time_months, co$status3,
          cov1 = as.matrix(co[, c("intervention", "income_k",
                                  "distance_km")]),
          failcode = 1, cencode = 0)
round(summary(fg)$conf.int, 2)

cuminc rows are labelled “group event”. For the ten TB patients (one group, labelled 1), the conversion CIF is 0.550 and the death CIF 0.325 at 12 weeks, as in the hand table. For the cohort, the CIF of dropout by 24 months is 0.476 without and 0.327 with the intervention (1 − KM gives 0.495 and 0.339); moving away reached 0.054 and 0.065. Tests gives Gray’s test comparing the groups’ CIFs: p = 0.011 for dropout, 0.69 for moving. crr fits the Fine–Gray model: the subdistribution HR for the intervention is 0.59 (0.41–0.85), close to the cause-specific 0.58 because moving is rare and shows no clear link to the intervention (Gray’s p = 0.69).

points.html: With competing events, 1 − KM overestimates the cumulative incidence. Use the CIF (Aalen–Johansen); F₁ + F₂ + S = 1.

Cause-specific HR (Cox, competing events censored): effect on the rate among those still at risk; suits aetiology. Subdistribution HR (Fine–Gray): effect on cumulative incidence; suits prognosis and planning. Report which one you used.
Decide at the design stage which events are censoring (the outcome could still happen, unseen) and which are competing (the outcome can no longer happen).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 14.5

questions.prompt: Five patients: event of interest at week 1, competing event at week 2, event of interest at week 3, censored at week 4, event of interest at week 5. Compute the CIF of the event of interest at week 3, and 1 − KM at week 3 with the competing event censored.
questions.answer:
CIF: week 1, 5 at risk, S(1₋) = 1: increment 1 × 1/5 = 0.200; S becomes 0.800. Week 2, competing event, 4 at risk: S = 0.800 × 3/4 = 0.600. Week 3, 3 at risk: increment 0.600 × 1/3 = 0.200. CIF(3) = 0.400.

1 − KM (competing event censored): week 1, 1 − 1/5 = 0.8; week 2, no step (censored); week 3, 3 at risk, × 2/3. KM = 0.8 × 2/3 = 0.533, so 1 − KM = 0.467. It overstates the probability of the event by 0.067, because it treats the patient with the competing event as though they could still have the event of interest.

questions.prompt: A district study of elderly patients after hip fracture asks (a) whether diabetes raises the rate of re-fracture among those still alive, and (b) what proportion of patients will re-fracture within two years, for service planning. Death is common. Which model suits each question?
questions.answer: 1. An aetiological question about the rate among those still at risk: the cause-specific hazard model (a Cox model for re-fracture with deaths censored). (b) A question about the actual proportion who re-fracture in a population where many die first: the cumulative incidence function (Aalen–Johansen), and, with covariates, the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard model. 1 − KM would overstate (b) because deaths are common.
